verses.text: Who has believed our message? To whom has the arm of Yahweh been revealed?
For he grew up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of dry ground. He has no good looks or majesty. When we see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
But he was pierced for our transgressions. He was crushed for our iniquities. The punishment that brought our peace was on him; and by his wounds we are healed.
All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
He was oppressed, yet when he was afflicted he didn’t open his mouth. As a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before its shearers is silent, so he didn’t open his mouth.
He was taken away by oppression and judgment; and as for his generation, who considered that he was cut off out of the land of the living and stricken for the disobedience of my people?
They made his grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death; although he had done no violence, nor was any deceit in his mouth.

Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he will see his offspring.  He will prolong his days, and Yahweh’s pleasure will prosper in his hand.
After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light  and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

Therefore will I give him a portion with the great, and he will divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was counted with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.

footnotes.content: The prophet asks the question that echoes through the ages: who truly receives this message of the suffering servant? It's a question each of us must answer for ourselves. The arm of the Lord—His power, His rescue—is revealed not in might and thunder, but in patient, willing suffering.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A tender plant in dry ground—the image captures something true about grace. There was nothing remarkable about His appearance to draw the eye or flatter the heart. He grew quietly, humbly, as a root seeking life in barren soil.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Despised and rejected—Isaiah names the real cost of His calling. 'A man of suffering' literally means one acquainted with disease, bearing the weight of human pain. Yet notice: even His rejection served us, though we didn't know it then.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We mistook Him. We thought He was cursed, cut off by God for His own failure. But He was bearing *our* sickness, shouldering what was *ours* to carry. The substitution is complete and tender—His weakness held our healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities—here is the heart of it, the turning point where the ancient word becomes flesh and blood. By His wounds we are healed. Not someday, not in theory: the healing is real, purchased at the deepest cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every sheep has wandered its own way—you, me, all of us. And the Lord, with a love that staggers the mind, gathered all that wandering into one, laying it on the one who stayed faithful. The innocence exchanged for our guilt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He opened not His mouth. In suffering, He was silent—not because He was defeated or overcome, but because He chose to bear it. Like a lamb led without protest, like a sheep before the shearers who makes no complaint. There is a dignity, a sovereign choice, in that silence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He was cut off out of the land of the living—separated, taken, stricken. Yet the verse speaks of His striving for the disobedience of His people. Even in His removal, His work was intercession, bearing the weight of our turning away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Assigned a grave with the wicked, yet buried in a rich man's tomb—the prophecy holds both shame and honor. Though He had done no violence and no deceit was in His mouth, He was treated as criminal and sinner. Innocent to the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: It pleased the Lord to bruise Him. Hard words, yet they speak of a purpose held together by love. His soul becomes an offering for sin, and from His suffering comes offspring—believers born again through His death. His death is not the end, but the seed of resurrection.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After suffering, He sees light and is satisfied. The righteous servant justifies many through knowledge of Himself—not by keeping score or demanding perfect obedience, but by revealing His steadfast love. He bears our iniquities as we know Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse that spans the ages: He poured out His soul unto death, was numbered with transgressors, yet interceded for them still. Looking back from our own time of grace, we recognize in His bearing the sin of many a portrait of the One who rose, who sits at the right hand asking forgiveness for those who pierced Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
